This brings us to another objection. If everything exists through God’s knowledge, will, and decree, then every part of the order and every particle in the universe must necessarily exist in relation to His eternal will. How, then, can the sacred report say, “I have never hesitated over anything I was going to do as I hesitated over taking the soul of My believing servant”? This is a difficult problem for anyone who wants to reconcile rational principles with religious teaching. No scholar has offered a fully satisfying answer. Our teacher suggests that hesitation is caused by competing reasons that favor each side. The cause is named by its effect: the meaning is that taking a believer’s life is good for the order of existence but painful for the believer. In other words, an act may be good in itself and necessary for many goods, while also being bad for some beings. This is what the report calls hesitation.

I say that this answer does not resolve the problem; it makes it harder. It places a conflict within the act itself, between doing it and leaving it undone. If neither side is stronger, choosing one would be unjustified. If one side is stronger, and God knows that it is stronger, then the act must follow from that knowledge; there is no hesitation. The answer that came to me is this: as we have explained, the natural world continually renews itself through substantial change. Every assumed part of something that unfolds gradually is preceded by a prior potentiality in matter. That potentiality is itself the earlier part of the thing.

There are two ways to speak of what is possible. We may consider what a thing is, without supposing that it must exist or must not exist. Or we may consider a real readiness in matter for a change that has not yet happened. In neither case is the outcome necessary simply because it is possible. In anything that comes into being gradually—motion, according to most philosophers, and bodily nature, as we have argued—each earlier stage contains the capacity for the next. Such a thing exists in a changing and incomplete way: what is present gives way to what has not yet come. But when the cause that produces a new stage acts, that stage must come to be. What was merely possible has then become real through the readiness that preceded it.

With this in mind, the things in this world belong to God’s detailed knowledge. In one respect they are His knowledge; in another, they are what He knows. As knowledge, each is a kind of hesitation within knowledge; as something known, each is a possibility in existence. Human souls, especially those of believers, contain more of these possibilities and changes than other beings, because they pass through many states of existence: nonliving, plant, animal, and then the stages beyond these. At last, through a divine power that takes souls from their bodies and draws their forms from matter, they leave these changes behind and reach holiness and lasting life.

Just as the mind can understand a form apart from the matter in which it appears, the Angel of Death and his helpers draw souls and forms out of their bodies and matter. Such changes occur in the material world, and also in the heavenly souls that are imprinted with forms and make up the Tablet of Effacement and Confirmation. Any detailed image written in those souls may be erased or changed: their level allows for this. What cannot change is God’s essence, His real attributes, the world of command, His prior decree, and His eternal knowledge. The Qur'an says, “God erases what He wills and confirms what He wills; with Him is the Mother of the Book.” That is the clear Tablet, protected from erasure and change. It contains all the beings that differ and even oppose one another in the outer world, gathered in a single, intellectual, luminous reality, free of conflict and opposition. The Qur'an says, “Not a leaf falls without His knowing it; there is no grain in the darkness of the earth, nothing fresh or dry, that is not in a clear Book.”

So the changes, new events, and limitations found in individual beings and natural things do not sever their connection to the First Reality or the divine oneness. Nor do they compromise God’s eternal will, which is free of possibility, or His true and timeless knowledge, which is free of doubt and hesitation. These changes occur at levels through which knowledge and will unfold.

Abū Naṣr says in Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam: “Pass into oneness, and you will be struck with wonder at eternity. If you ask about it, oneness casts its shadow, and the whole comes into being. The pen writes creation on the tablet.” He also says: “The first knowledge is of God’s essence, and it is not divided. The second knowledge comes from His essence; when it becomes many, the multiplicity is not in His essence but after His essence. Not a leaf falls without His knowing it. From there, the pen writes on the tablet without end.” He says again: “Oneness beheld itself, then beheld power, and the second knowledge followed, containing multiplicity. From there, the world of command begins; the pen writes it on the tablet, and unity becomes many.”
XIII. How to understand scriptural references to God’s hesitation and testing, and to a change in what is decreed

This also concerns the response to prayers and the rescue of people in distress, when these things occur alongside their requests and without the usual natural causes. Know that the divine reality has different levels, and the most beautiful names of God have their own manifestations. We have discussed part of this in earlier stages of the First Journey.

In the layers of heaven, God has angelic servants whose level is that of souls, below the rank of the foremost and nearest beings. The latter belong to the world of command, which is free of change and renewal. Though the angelic servants are below them, all their actions obey God and are done at His command. They do not disobey Him in anything they do, will, imagine, desire, or inwardly incline toward. Whoever is like this acts in keeping with the Real and speaks truthfully: there is no desire in them that conflicts with God’s desire. Their will is absorbed in His will, and their choice in His choice.

Their obedience to God is like the way our senses obey the soul. They cannot act against what the soul wants, and they do not need to be commanded, forbidden, encouraged, or restrained. As soon as our rational soul intends a sensory action, the sense carries out that intention. The senses belong to a different level from the rational soul; they are lower in the inner world. In the same way, the angels in heaven obey God. Their very being makes them obedient to His command. With their inner hearing they listen to His revelation, and with their luminous hearts they feel His greatness. They are in awe of His beauty and majesty. They cannot rebel or disobey; they do what they are commanded. Their movements, stillness, thoughts, and images all arise through the Real and from the Real. This is the first principle.

A second principle: something can come about in a receptive body through its own capacities, through external causes, or through bodily arrangements. Heat, for example, may enter a body suited to receive it when an external source such as fire warms it. But something may also come about in a body without any material readiness or receptive capacity, through a higher cause and an inner source. A person’s body may become extremely hot because the soul pictures something frightening or stirs up anger, without any external source of heat. A person’s limbs may grow cold through fear, without a natural or external cause. And imagining something desired can move the limbs and produce moisture, even without the body’s usual fullness or natural preparation.

The matter of the world—the body of the great human being—can likewise be affected by the soul that governs it. Rare events may occur in the world without following the usual natural course or arising from the natural causes that ordinarily prepare for them. The earlier causes may even work against the result, or be suited to produce its opposite. This is why such events are rare and astonishing. This is the second principle.

Once these two principles are understood, we can say that every inscription in the heavenly tablets and records of destiny is also written by the First Reality, following the prior decree written by the Highest Pen in the Preserved Tablet. The heavenly records and tablets of destiny—the active angels’ hearts and the souls that govern the heavens—are all tablets of erasure and confirmation. The images written in their hearts, natures, and souls may disappear or change, because their level allows for change. As we have explained in discussing the world’s coming-to-be and the renewal of nature, souls, and other powers connected to bodies, only God’s essence, His real attributes, the world of command, His prior decree, and His eternal knowledge are beyond change.

Scripture speaks of God as hesitating through these records and the angels who write in them. A report says, “I have never hesitated over anything I was going to do.” Scripture also speaks of God testing people: “We tested them with good and bad things,” “We test what you do,” and “Until We know which of you strive and remain steadfast.” The angel who records these divine decrees is noble, as the Qur'an says: “Noble scribes.” God dictates to that angel in a way suited to His care, which is free of change or coming into being. Without these receptive souls, where forms of will and knowledge can renew and earlier records can be replaced, everything would be fixed once and for all. The flow of divine generosity would be limited to a set number of things, the path by which seekers rise from the lower world to the higher would be closed, and no one could draw near to God after the darkness of distance.

In short, without this, the stages by which every being returns to God would be impossible. Rational principles rule this out, and divine care does not allow it. So the renewal of knowledge and states in some angels—the noble scribes—is possible, not impossible or far-fetched.

When a prophet or saint connects with these records and reads what God has revealed and written in the heart, that person can tell others what they have seen with the eye of the heart and heard with the ear of the heart: the sound of those noble pens. Their words are true and direct, unlike the words of astrologers and fortune-tellers, who speak without certain, direct insight, relying instead on experience, guesswork, and the like.

When the prophet or saint connects to these records again, they may see something different from what they saw before—something unlike the earlier forms and unlike the natural causes then present in the heavens and on earth. This is called abrogation, a change in what is decreed, or something similar. No heavenly or earthly soul can know it except through God, who keeps this knowledge to Himself. No natural cause brings it about, nor can it be inferred beforehand from the images and patterns already recorded. This is why reports from our Imāmī tradition quote Abū ʿAbd Allāh as saying, “God has two kinds of knowledge: a hidden, guarded knowledge that no one knows but Him. From this knowledge comes a change in what is decreed. He also has a knowledge He has taught to His angels, messengers, and prophets, and we know it.”

Abū Jaʿfar is also reported to have said: “There are two kinds of knowledge. One is kept by God, hidden from every creature. The other He teaches to His angels, messengers, and prophets. What He teaches them will surely happen; God does not contradict Himself, nor do His angels or messengers. But from the knowledge He keeps hidden, He brings forward, delays, or confirms whatever He wills.”

In his book The Beginning and the Return, in a section on how earthly beings are governed and on kinds that are not preserved, Avicenna says that this care does not come from the First or from the separate intellects. It must come from a later source: either a soul spread through the world of coming-to-be and decay, or a heavenly soul. Most people, he thinks, would say that it is a soul generated by the intellects and heavenly souls, especially the soul of the Sun or of the inclined sphere. It governs what lies beneath the Moon with the help of heavenly bodies and the light of the active intellect. In any case, this source of care must perceive individual things. Avicenna therefore thinks it is more likely to be a heavenly soul, able to imagine and sense events in a way suited to its own body.

When an event occurs, this soul understands the perfection the event needs and the way to bring it about. Its understanding then gives rise to the corresponding form in matter. The soul that answers those who pray and ask for help may be this one. Avicenna says this seems likely: when the soul sees matter changing, it understands the good order and perfection that should be there. What it understands then comes to be.

It may also perceive changes in the lives of those who dwell in this world and understand what must be done to remove a lack or evil and bring about good. The event then follows that understanding. Such a soul cares for every lack and evil that enters this world and its parts, so that good and order may follow. This care should not be confined to one thing and excluded from another. If a prayer is not answered or an evil is not removed, there is some hidden evil that we do not see, or divine care does not require its removal.

In another section, Avicenna describes rare events that come from this soul and even change nature. Since the soul’s understanding is followed by forms in matter, it is possible for a wrongdoer to die, a good person to be saved, or an unusual fire, earthquake, or other event to occur. A natural material may cool when it is hot, warm when it is cold, move when it is still, or become still when it is moving—not through its usual natural causes, but through the new natural cause that arises from this higher source. Animals or plants that ordinarily come from reproduction may also come about in other ways, with new forms unlike those of their usual parents. Such things follow from the understanding of this soul. We should not reject unfamiliar events in the world’s governance; rare and astonishing events have causes of the kind he has described.

Avicenna then tells a story he had heard. A physician attended the court of a Samanid ruler and was so trusted that he was invited to dine in the women’s quarters. No men entered there; female servants brought the food. One day a servant carrying the meal bent over from a sudden bout of gas and could not straighten up. The ruler asked the physician to treat her at once. The physician had no natural treatment that could cure her so quickly, so he turned to a psychological remedy. He first ordered that her hair be uncovered, but it had no effect. He then ordered that her belly be uncovered, still without effect. Finally, he ordered that she be uncovered below. As the women moved to do this, a strong heat rose in her body, dispersed the gas, and she sprang up, well again.
XIV. A fuller account of answered prayers and how to resolve the objection

Once you see clearly that all beings depend on God’s will, power, and care—His knowledge of the good in the order of things—you can also see that the parts of this order are connected and that effects follow their causes. Among the causes that bring events about is the presence of someone who calls on God and their prayer. Just as a person’s existence, knowledge, power, will, and choice are among the causes of an action, prayer, asking, persistence, and humility before God are among the causes by which a request is granted and what is sought comes about, by God’s permission and through His realm.

Prayer may reach the world of command and affect the hearing of the angels in heaven. As we said in the previous chapter, there is a soul-like being in the heavens that can be affected by earthly events and can in turn affect the earth: it warms what is cold, cools what is hot, moves what is still, stills what is moving, and changes one element into another, with help from above and support from the light of the intellectual beings. It is affected by the illnesses and calamities it observes in this world, unless they are balanced by what brings good and well-being. In its receptive soul and intellect, it forms an understanding of what must be done to remove evil and bring about good.

This being is not purely an active intellect, unaffected by anything, nor is it purely passive, unable to affect anything except through help from above. It acts on what is below it and is also affected by what is below it. So it may be moved by the prayers of people in distress and the cries of those in need, and may answer them by God’s permission, meet their needs, and grant their requests.

We have already said that only the universal intellectual world of command is wholly free of change and response to anything else. The principle that a higher being is not affected by a lower one applies only to what is higher in every respect, or to what is higher in the very respect in question. But a soul-like being—even one of the heavens—can be affected by some earthly events, especially by the noble rational souls among us. It may turn toward them, help fulfill their requests, and answer their prayers. This does not conflict with its being higher than them in other respects.

For this reason, the claim in Avicenna’s Notes that the heavenly beings cannot be affected by earthly beings needs qualification. He says that we may imagine that the heavens are affected by us when we pray and they answer, even though we are their effects and they are our causes. But, as we have explained, this is not always true. Do not follow those who know truth only through the authority of other people.

Now consider the objection: if what we ask for has already been set down in the eternal decree and written in the divine measure, why go to the trouble of asking for it? And if it has not been written there, why ask for something that cannot happen? The answer is that asking and praying are also part of the decree and measure: they are among the causes and conditions that bring about the very thing decreed. Whenever God decrees that something happen, He also decrees its causes and conditions; otherwise, He has not decreed it. When God wills a thing, He prepares its causes. Among the causes of the thing we pray for are the caller’s prayer, humility, and need.

Prayer and remembrance are to the fulfillment of our requests in the world what thought and reflection are to the discovery of conclusions and knowledge in the mind. So prayers and invocations are channels flowing from the sea of decree and streams flowing from the rivers of destiny.

Avicenna writes in his Notes that a prayer is answered when its causes coincide in keeping with divine wisdom. The cause of someone’s prayer and the cause of the thing they ask for both come from God and meet at the right time. Could the thing have happened without the prayer? No: the same God made the prayer a cause for the thing, just as He made medicine a cause of recovery. A sick person does not recover without taking the medicine; in the same way, the requested event does not come without the prayer that is meant to bring it about. For a reason, God brings the prayer and the event together as He has decreed. Prayer is necessary, and so is expecting an answer. God causes us to pray, and our prayer becomes a cause of the answer, meeting with the event it was made to bring about.

Sometimes a person’s prayer is not answered, even when the goal they seek seems beneficial. The reason, Avicenna says, is that a beneficial goal must serve the order of the whole, not only what that person wants. What seems beneficial to the individual may not truly be so. In that case, the prayer is not answered.

He also says that when a pure soul prays, the First Reality may give it power to affect the elements, which then respond and change according to its will. This is one way a prayer is answered. We can see something similar in our own bodies: imagining something may change the body in keeping with the soul’s state and images. A soul may also affect a body other than its own or another person’s soul, as in stories about the powers of imagination among Indian sages, if those stories are true. The first principles may respond to such a soul when it asks for something that benefits the whole order.

Avicenna says that no prayer is impossible to answer. It can be known to God, even if He knows it through the person who prays. Whatever is known to Him can exist, provided that no other known thing prevents it. For example, someone may pray for another person to perish, expecting that this will happen if their bodily balance is ruined. But God may also know from another cause that the person’s balance must remain sound. Then the prayer cannot be answered. “From another cause” means from the causes that keep the body balanced. If God knows through those causes that the body need not remain sound, there is no opposing cause, and the prayer can be answered. That is why no one should pray for another person’s ruin: God already knows that the prayer will be made, and whatever He knows can happen.

Avicenna also says that the First Reality is the cause of all things known to Him and of their necessity, but in an ordered way. He is the cause of causes, and so the cause of what He knows. In one respect, He knows one thing before another; in another, one thing is the cause of His knowing another. For example, He is the cause of knowing the First Intellect, and the First Intellect is the cause of knowing what follows from it. So, although He is the cause of knowing the First Intellect and its effects, in a certain respect the First Intellect becomes the cause of His knowing its own effects. Prayer works in the same way. God is the true cause of the prayer and of the person who prays. Then the person’s prayer becomes the cause of God’s knowing that prayer. In this respect the person is a cause of God’s knowing the prayer, though in truth the person does not affect God; God is the one who causes it. This is the end of Avicenna’s account in the Notes.

As we will explain later, the philosophers say that the souls of the heavenly bodies know the consequences, aims, longings, and motives of their movements. Everything that exists in this world—substances, qualities, forms, and matter—has its shape, arrangement, and measure set in another world between the world of pure intellects and intellectual forms, and the world of natural bodies and material forms. In his books, including The Healing and The Directives and Remarks, Avicenna says that heavenly souls and higher beings know particular things. Our changing thoughts and acts of will have earthly and heavenly causes that meet and bring them about. The same is true of natural events that arise after not existing, and of events forced upon things. These causes crowd together and clash, yet their ongoing interaction forms an order beneath the movement of the heavens.

When the first heavenly causes know their own effects and the way they lead to the next causes, they also know what follows from them. Heavenly souls have some power to act on particular meanings and to perceive particular images, as well as universal meanings and the separate intellects they resemble. They can perceive events through the separate details of their active and receptive causes and what follows from them. These causes ultimately lead to a natural or voluntary cause that is decisive, not merely a passing desire.

Every act of will comes into being after not existing and has causes that meet and bring it about. It does not arise from yet another act of will, which would lead to an endless chain, nor from the agent’s nature alone, which would make the will arise whenever that nature is present. Rather, a will arises when causes and motives come together from both earthly and heavenly sources and make it necessary. Nature, if it is already present, is a basic source; if it has newly arisen, it must also depend on earthly and heavenly causes.

Avicenna concludes that heavenly souls know particular things, while what lies above them knows particulars in a universal way. The heavenly souls know them directly, or through what reaches a direct perceiver, or as things seen by the senses. They know what will happen and, in many cases, which of two possible outcomes is more fitting, more beneficial, and closer to pure good.

We have explained that the images understood by these causes give rise to the forms found here. If such an outcome is possible and there are no stronger heavenly causes opposing it, then it must come about—not from an earthly cause or an ordinary natural cause in heaven, but through the influence of these events on heavenly things. Strictly speaking, they do not themselves cause the effect. Its cause is the heavenly source of its existence. When the heavenly source understands the first causes, it understands what follows from them, including which possible outcome is better. Once it understands that outcome, it brings it about, unless an opposing cause prevents it.

For example, heat might arise even though no earthly source is heating the body. The heavenly soul understands that warmth is good and produces an image of it. This is like the way a person’s thoughts may warm their own body. Or an earthly cooling cause may be present. The heavenly image of the good that comes from warmth can overcome it, just as an angry person’s thoughts can overcome the cooling effect in their body. Events of this kind are changes, not ordinary natural processes. They may be inspirations that reach the person who asks, or someone else, or a mixture of events that leads to a useful result. Prayer calls for this power as thought calls for understanding; both ultimately come from above.

This is not the source of heavenly images themselves. The First Reality knows all of this in the way proper to Him, and all events begin from Him, though they come about through intermediaries. Prayer and offerings can therefore bring benefit, especially in asking for rain and other needs. We should fear the consequences of evil and hope for the reward of good: this is a deterrent from evil, and its truth becomes clear through particular events. The heavenly sources understand this, so it must also have a real existence. If it does not happen, there is an evil we do not understand or another cause that prevents it; in that case, the other outcome is more fitting than the one we asked for.

Avicenna adds that we can see how things understood to be beneficial and useful come to exist in nature in this way by looking at the uses of organs in animals and plants. Each is made for its purpose, though no ordinary natural cause explains how that purpose was first set. Its source must be divine care. So we should accept that these things exist through the same kind of care.

He also says that the causes of our prayers, charity, injustice, and sin all lead back to nature, will, and chance. Nature has its source in the divine realm. Our wills arise after not existing, and everything that comes into being has a cause. Our wills are caused by earthly and heavenly events, which together bring them about. Chance occurs when these causes meet. When we trace everything back, we reach first principles established by God. His decree is the first simple arrangement; measure is its gradual unfolding, as the meeting of simple causes produces particular results. This is the end of Avicenna’s account.

I have followed Avicenna’s words closely because they contain much that is useful about how events that come into being are linked to God’s will, knowledge, and care, without attributing change, passivity, or a low purpose to Him. Still, his account needs to be completed in two ways.

First, he avoids saying that anything in the heavens can be affected by something on earth. Yet we have often heard of—and seen—rain, earthquakes, sinkholes, and similar acts of mercy or punishment occurring alongside the prayers of devout people and the requests of those in need. We also hear of events connected with prophets and saints that make it clear that some heavenly source and some of God’s angels respond to events among people on earth: they hear their prayers and turn toward answering them. Several Qur'anic verses say this plainly and cannot be explained away. God says to Noah, “Build the Ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation,” and to Moses and Aaron, “Do not fear; I am with you. I hear and see.” To the final Prophet He says, “When We recite it, follow its recitation; then it is for Us to make it clear.”

Second, Avicenna does not accept that the beings of this world exist in a higher world as immaterial forms, free from matter, limitation, possibility, evil, nonexistence, and darkness. He criticizes those who affirm such separate forms, including Plato, Socrates, and earlier masters of knowledge and wisdom. We have already established their existence through philosophical explanation and proof. Avicenna should have explained how events that come into being connect to the world of destiny and correspond to it, just as a perfect copy matches its model. He should also have explained how the world of destiny connects to the simple world of decree, matches it, and is one with it. He could not do so because he denied that the simple intellect is one with all the things it understands, and did not see that a truly simple reality must contain all things. Nothing in heaven or earth escapes it.

For this reason, Avicenna treats God’s knowledge of things as a collection of qualities and images residing in Him. He then says that, though they are qualities in Him, they do not affect or complete Him because they follow His essence rather than precede it. His perfection and glory lie in their flowing from Him, not in their existing for Him. You have already seen the limits and flaws in this account. God is the source of generosity and grace.

The life we know in this world involves awareness and action. For most animals, awareness means sensation, and action means movement through space, arising from desire. These two effects come from two different powers, one that perceives and one that moves. But if a being’s awareness were higher than sensation—intellect, for example—and its action were nobler than directly causing movement—bringing things into existence, for example—then it would have an even better claim to be called living.

And if the very same simple reality were the source both of its awareness and its action, so that its awareness were itself its action and creative power, it would have an even stronger claim to that name, since it would be free of composition. Composition requires possibility and dependence: a composite thing depends on something else to hold it together. Possibility is a kind of absence opposed to existence, and death is opposed to life. The truly living being is therefore one whose powers are not assembled from parts.

We have shown that the Necessary Being is simple in reality, one in essence and attribute, and utterly one in power. His very understanding of things is their coming from Him. One simple reality is the intellect of all things and the source of all things. He therefore has a greater and more fitting claim to the name “living” than any other living being. He gives life to all things and gives existence—and the perfections of existence, such as knowledge and power—to everything that exists.

Consider an image of knowledge that arises in us and then leads us to make something. If the image alone were enough to produce the made thing—if the image itself were already the active source of what it represents—then our knowing would be the same as our power to make. We would be able to make whatever we know, and what we know would be one and the same as what we make. But that is not the case. We often know things we desire but cannot bring about.

Even for something we can make, such as writing, knowing what it is does not by itself make it real. We also need a fresh act of will, arising from desire. These together set the moving power to work. That power moves the nerves and bodily organs; the organs move external tools; and those tools act on the material we work with, such as paper or a board. So in us, knowledge is not itself power or will. Power begins with the source of movement. Nor is will itself power, or power itself action: power is the capacity to act and bring something about. The image first stirs desire and will; they move the power; the power moves the bodily instrument; and that instrument moves what it acts upon. Each of these movers is itself moved, because each is mixed with limitation, lack, and possibility.

If any one of them were complete and powerful in its own way, it would not need the others in order to act. If our mental image were vivid and complete enough, for example, it could itself give rise to the action and bring it about. As we have said, God’s knowledge of the most complete order is itself His will. His power is His essence understanding all things—not as something learned from them, but as the source of them all. This first intellect is also His eternal will, free of any aim beyond itself, and the existence of all beings follows from it, just as loving someone also leads us to love what belongs to them. God loves everything He creates because He loves His own essence. This is His will, free of every flaw. Anyone who believes otherwise has left the right path and misunderstood God’s attributes and names.

This is also how we must understand God as living: He is the one who perceives and acts. We have explained what perception and action mean; in Him, they are one reality, though we can speak of them under different descriptions.

As we have explained, God’s essential attributes all exist through one existence, and He deserves their names because their meanings truly apply to Him. His relational attributes also return to one relation. The same existence in Him is knowledge, power, and life; and when related to what He creates, it is called knowing, creating, providing, making, and willing. If you understand the principles we have set out, you will see that the first attribute of the Necessary Being is simply that He exists: pure existence, without any essence or limitation mixed into it. Other attributes either mean this existence together with a relation, or this existence considered without something that does not belong to it. None of them introduces multiplicity into His essence.

When we call Him “one,” we mean this existence without any division—whether into measurable parts, real parts such as matter and form, or conceptual parts such as broader kind and difference. When we call Him “one and unique,” we mean that this existence has no partner in its kind or in its necessity. When we call Him intellect, knower, and known, we mean that this existence is free of the possibility of being mixed with matter and its attachments, while also standing in a relation to what it knows. This is the account found in The Healing.

In our view, the negative element is not part of the meaning of perception or understanding, even if it follows from it in reality. Perception means that something exists for, or is present to, another. Matter and material things are not present to themselves or to another in this way. Because they are bound up with their own limited existence, they remain unknown unless another image of them is present to the knower. The stronger the existence, the stronger the perception. The strongest forms of existence are the intellectual images, in degrees of strength, followed by images in imagination and then images in the senses. When existence becomes so weak that it takes material form, it is hidden from perception and cannot be grasped or made present to the knower.

When we call God “the First,” we mean that this existence is related to all things as their active source. When we call Him “the Last,” we mean that it is related to them as their final aim. When we call Him “powerful,” we mean that the necessary existence of everything else follows from Him.
When we call Him “living,”we mean this existence considered together with its relation to the intelligible forms of all things as their knower and maker.

As for the life of every living thing, it is a way of existing: a being is alive when it can perform the actions of living things, which arise from knowledge and power. But some beings need an additional state before they can act in this way, while others do not.

The first kind includes living bodies. They become capable of life only after another state has come about in them. If a body’s existence were already the very same as its ability to perform the actions of life, every body would be alive. If that ability comes to a body later, it does not come simply because it is a body, but because of something else that distinguishes it. Nor can you say that this new state—the ability to act in a living way—is what makes the body exist at all. That would apply only to body considered as a general kind, not to body considered as matter. We are discussing the essence of body itself, apart from what is added to it. The existence a body has simply as a body is not connected with animal life. That life is something added to it.

The second kind is what lies beyond bodies. In beings that are not bodies, their existence may itself be their capacity for life; in most cases, it must be so. Separate substances and immaterial forms have this character: their existence itself is their life. They are not made up of matter and form, since their formal existence is not tied to something merely potential. Life in them is not something added that makes them alive; it is simply their being alive. Otherwise, the thing would have to become alive through the very existence it already has, which would make it depend on itself, or else on another existence. That would contradict the assumption that it exists apart from matter, where one state comes after another. And if we then asked about that added existence, we would be led into an endless chain. As we have explained in discussing existence, relation, place, and continuity, life and the like are ways of existing. The Necessary Being, whose reality is simple, has an even greater claim to have life identical with His existence.

The meaning of “life” differs from the meanings of “knowledge” and “power.”Life is in a way their source. Many later thinkers, not distinguishing meaning from reality, have disagreed about whether life in God is another attribute added to perception and action. They then relied on scripture to establish that He is living, saying that reason alone does not establish this attribute.

The truth is that life, like the other attributes of perfection, is a perfection of existence simply as existence. Whatever is a perfection of existence without being limited to a particular kind of nature, size, or number must belong to the source of existence and its giver. The source that gives existence and its perfections has the strongest claim to that perfection.

Still, the meaning of life is not the same as the meanings of knowledge and power. One can imagine a living being that, at a given time, knows nothing and performs no action. It would still be alive. In us, life is the state from which awareness and action arise. The powers of awareness and action are like instruments of this state, which is their source. This cannot apply to God, who is far above different powers and inner instruments. His life, like His knowledge, power, and will, exists at the same level, as one reality with one identity. Yet the meaning of life differs from that of knowledge; both differ from power, and power differs from will. Proof establishes this perfection in God in a higher and nobler way, just as it establishes His knowledge, power, and will in a higher and nobler way.

One clarification: Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi says in his treatise on knowledge that people wanted to describe God by the better of two opposites. Since they called Him knowing and powerful, and found that anything without life could not be described by these terms, they also called Him living—especially since life is nobler than its opposite, death. This reasoning is flawed and incomplete. Not everything nobler than its opposite can be attributed to God. Solidity is nobler than softness, motion than rest, and the sphere is the noblest of shapes. To attribute a perfection to God, it must be a basic attribute of existence as such. Otherwise, it cannot belong to Him.

The divine philosopher, when establishing that God is living, must first give a meaning of life that can be a perfection of existence in general. It must not depend on a special capacity or on belonging to one kind of being, nor may it bring multiplicity, change, or dependence on anything else. Once life is understood in this way, it can be attributed to the Necessary Being, the source of all other beings and their perfections. The giver of perfection has a greater claim to it than anything else.

Al-Tusi also cites a report from one of the Imams: “Was He called knowing and powerful for any reason other than that He gave knowledge to those who know and power to those who are powerful? Whatever you can imagine, however subtle, is a created thing like you and belongs to you. God is the giver of life and the ordainer of death. Perhaps tiny ants imagine that God has two horns like theirs, and think that anyone without them is deficient. That is how people are when they describe God. God is the one to whom we turn for refuge.” This report is noble and true. It points toward the way we have established God’s attributes of perfection: He gives knowledge, power, and life, which are perfections of existence as such. When a perfection exists in a caused thing, it must exist in its cause in a higher and nobler way.

The report also says that human understanding cannot reach the full reality of the attributes we use of God. This applies not only to life but to all His attributes. The real attributes stand in the same relation as existence and necessity. Just as existence is necessary in God while the meaning of existence is shared by all beings, so there is knowledge that exists necessarily in God while the meaning of knowledge is shared by eternal and created knowledge. The same holds for power, will, and all the real attributes whose meanings apply both to God and to possible beings.

Yet there are people who know the truth through the truth itself and know God’s attributes through His attributes, not by comparing them with created beings. They have gone beyond the ordinary state of the soul, left behind their separate selves, and awakened to the final reality. They see what others do not see.

Our true religious law teaches—and this is among the basic truths of our clear faith, known from the Qur'an, widely transmitted reports, and the community’s consensus—that the Creator hears and sees. Scholars have differed over whether hearing and sight fall under knowledge in general, meaning knowledge of things heard and seen, or whether they are two attributes distinct from knowledge.
Station Six: God hears and sees

Some theologians, including the leading Imami scholars among our own teachers and the scholar al-Tusi, as well as al-Ashʿarī and his followers, agree here with most philosophers. Those philosophers deny that God knows particulars or anything other than Himself in the specific, direct way in which such things are present to Him. These scholars therefore explain hearing and sight as forms of knowledge: hearing is knowledge of what is heard, and sight is knowledge of what is seen.
Station Six: God hears and sees

Others treat hearing and sight as two kinds of sensory perception. They do so either because they believe God has a body or directly contacts bodies—God is far above what wrongdoers say—or because they believe that, since God has no limitation or need, He can sense without an organ, even though our limited condition requires one. This claim is unclear. If a deeply learned sage made it, it might have a sound meaning. But many theologians and debaters have not seen that sensing by itself points to a limitation in both the one who senses and the thing sensed.
Station Six: God hears and sees

In short, either God’s hearing and sight mean sensory awareness in the ordinary sense, or they mean His general knowledge of things that can be heard and seen. The truth is that hearing and sight mean something different from knowledge in general. They are two specific kinds of knowledge beyond it. If their meanings can apply to everything that exists, simply as something that exists, without implying a body, change, or being affected, then we must affirm them of God.
Station Six: God hears and sees

You have already learned that sensation alone does not make a thing particular or individual. What makes it individual is its own distinct way of existing. Existence and individuality are one in reality, though we use different words for them. You have also learned that God knows external things as individuals: their own existence is their presence before Him and their being known to Him. His direct, illuminating awareness of things heard and seen goes beyond His general knowledge of them, even when that general knowledge is universal, as it is when He knows them through concepts. Directly witnessing what is heard is hearing; directly witnessing what is seen is sight. So His hearing and sight cannot be reduced to knowledge in general. Indeed, it would be closer to the truth to say the reverse, as the Illuminationist master did: God’s knowledge returns to His sight, rather than His sight to His knowledge.
Station Six: God hears and sees
Station Six: God hears and sees

What sight really is differs from what most people think. It does not happen when an image of the thing seen is imprinted on the eye and affects it, as natural philosophers say. Nor does it happen when a beam travels in a cone between the eye and the thing seen, whether that beam is a physical body or something else. And it does not happen, as the Illuminationist master held, because the soul gains direct awareness of a material image through the body and its position in relation to that image. We reject all these accounts, as we explain elsewhere.
Station Six: God hears and sees

In our view, sight happens when the soul brings an image into being and that image is present to it in the world of images. This image is free of natural matter. The soul relates to it as a maker relates to what it makes, not as something that receives a quality and is perfected by it.
Station Six: God hears and sees

Sight still depends on the eye, on a natural image, on a certain position between them, on the absence of anything blocking them, and on other conditions. But these are not needed because sight is impossible without them; otherwise, we could not see in sleep. They are needed because the soul is weak at the beginning of its life and depends on bodily matter, both for its existence and for its perceptions.
Station Six: God hears and sees

The soul’s existence is not the same as the body’s, even though it depends on the body. In the same way, sight does not take place through the eye, even though it depends on the eye. As the soul can eventually do without the natural body after reaching a certain level of maturity, it can also come to perceive particular things visually without relying on the organs or their physical effects. We have explained this fully in our discussion of the soul. Anyone who looks at the matter fairly and clearly will see that sight can occur without an organ or its being affected, and without the soul itself being affected, because the soul makes the images it sees; it does not receive them from elsewhere.
Station Six: God hears and sees

Once we establish that a soul free from the natural world can perceive particular visual images through its own sight—which is identical with its own being—we can see that sight, in general, belongs to anything that exists simply as something that exists. It does not require a body, change, or being affected. Sight is a perfection, and lacking it is a deficiency. God is more worthy of this perfection than anything else.
Station Six: God hears and sees

The same is true of hearing. People commonly say that hearing happens when sound strikes or tears through the air, which must then ripple toward a cartilage organ lined with nerves. The moving air affects the soul, which wakes to the sounds, letters, and words and perceives them. But this account is not correct.
Station Six: God hears and sees

Some of the greatest sages have said that the heavens make beautiful sounds and noble melodies as they move. They say that Pythagoras rose to them himself and heard their lovely music with a subtle mind, then wrote the science of music.
Station Six: God hears and sees

We can see that hearing does not always require a natural organ or moving air because a person may hear a loud sound in sleep, such as thunder, and be deeply affected by it—no less than by a sound heard while awake. In sleep, the soul is connected to another world. Our discussion of speech will make the truth of this clear, God willing. Praise belongs to God, at the beginning and at the end. This completes the first part of Divine Philosophy. The second part follows in the Seventh Station, on God’s being the speaker, and on the truths contained in the discussion of speech and the Book.

The opening praise uses many kinds of beauty in its words and meaning: for example, fitting the introduction to the subject and book, and pairing opposite or related ideas. It brings together God's being, attributes, actions, and effects; light, shining, rays, and appearing; bringing into being, creating, making, and forming; intellects, souls, bodies, forms, and readiness; and pages, writing, words, reading, revelation, and clear and hidden meanings. The same pattern continues in the lines of thanks and blessings that follow. Calling God the “Necessary Being” and saying that He shines with light also points to the different language used by Aristotle’s school and the philosophers of illumination. The first speak of God as necessary and true existence; the second call Him the Light of Lights and the self-sufficient light. — س قده

By calling the intelligences “lasting,” the author means that their essences are lasting, since their existence is a ray from God's own being. The same applies to souls. He says that the intelligences come from the ray of God's being, but describes the souls as coming from His attributes because intellects belong to the divine realm, while souls are also connected to the world of images. Another possibility is that “attributes” here means God's active qualities, which are the intelligences. — س قده

“Motions” means the stages by which beings grow toward perfection. “Causes” means earthly causes, since the author has already named the souls and bodies of the heavens. It is better to add new information than repeat what has been said. Also, “forming” usually means bringing something into being after matter and time already exist. The heavenly spheres are created directly; they are not formed from prior matter. — س قده

The Prophet's gift of words that gather great meaning reflects the way his revealed Qur'an gathers all the words of existence in the outer and inner worlds. His spiritual reality is the Universal Intellect, which gathers all the higher and lower intellects. The human intellects of this world were made from what remained of his clay. The letters Ya-Sin in revelation also point to the all-embracing nature of the final complete human being: the letter Ya points to the ten levels of descent and ascent, and Sin, whose written form and sound are balanced, points to the complete human being, whose knowing and acting powers are balanced. In this way, all ten levels of existence are gathered in the human being. — س قده

Here “general knowledge” means the broad study of existence and the broad sense of divine philosophy. It considers the Necessary Being and possible beings in general, as ideas. The more specific study of divine philosophy considers the reality named by the idea “Necessary Being”: it proves that God exists and studies His attributes and actions. A person may know some features of a thing while still doubting that the thing exists. For example, one may be certain that the maker of the world would be knowing, powerful, and willing, yet still doubt that such a maker exists. — س قده

The author says “fellow human beings,” not “offspring of the same species,” because he means people in the ordinary sense. He may also be hinting at the point established later: inwardly, humanity is one kind; outwardly, it appears as different kinds. — س قده

The early philosophers said instead that God's giving never stops, His words never run out, and His light never sets. The world depends on Him forever. But they did not deny that the world began or came to an end. Religious thinkers use the world's beginning to prove its maker, and its passing away to explain judgment and the reaching of final goals. So a seeker of wisdom should not say, “I learned one thing but missed many others.”
